785.title: Four, five times
785.hook: Uttama left her cell again and again, restless, until the day she stayed (Therigatha, Uttama)
785.howItsDone: Some meditation teachers describe noticing the wandering mind and returning to the breath as the heart of sitting practice, and Uttama's verse is read as an honest account of restlessness on the way to stillness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mutta, freed from mortar, pestle and crooked husband. Your line was so freed. Which freedom did you name? Day seven hundred eighty-five.

A door opens. A nun steps out of her small dwelling and stands there. She can't settle. She goes back in and sits. Before long she's on her feet and out again. The Therigatha doesn't hide this, and neither does she. In her own poem a nun named Uttama counts it: four times, five times, she went out of her dwelling, with no peace of mind and her thoughts out of her control. It's an honest number. Not once. Not a hundred. Four, five. Today, the number she remembered, and what came after it.
screen: `A DOOR OPENS.` → `OUT, AND BACK, AND OUT.` → `FOUR, FIVE TIMES.`

segments.voice: First, the leaving. Uttama's poem begins with restlessness, plainly told. She had gone forth. She had a place to sit. And she kept getting up. The restlessness wasn't something she'd outgrown before she joined. It came with her into the robe. Second, the help. Then, the poem says, she went to a nun she could trust. That nun taught her the dhamma: how a person is made of changing parts, the senses and their objects, the elements. Uttama didn't solve her restlessness alone in her room. She went and asked someone. Third, the sitting. Having heard the teaching, she did what she'd been asked. And the poem says she sat in one posture for seven days, steeped in joy and ease. Fourth, the darkness broken. On the eighth day, the poem says, she stretched out her legs, having torn through the mass of darkness. The same picture as Punna's poem: wisdom breaking the dark. So the shape of Uttama's poem is out, out, out, then help, then stillness. The four and five times aren't cut from the story to make her look better. They're the first line. The tradition kept the count of her leavings right beside the moment she came free, as if the leaving were part of the path that led to the staying. And the staying came after the help, not instead of the leaving.
screen: `OUT OF THE ROOM, AGAIN.` · `A NUN SHE COULD TRUST.` · `SHE SAT, AND STAYED.` · `THE DARKNESS BROKEN.` · then, large: `SHE STAYED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: return to the cushion once more. Settle, wherever you are; a chair works as well as a cushion. During the sit, the mind may leave. It may leave four times, five times, more. Each time you see it has gone, come back to the breath. Don't count the leaving as failure. Uttama's poem counts it plainly and goes on. Out, and back. Out, and back. The coming back is the practice. The bell holds the time.
Four. Four times, five times, Uttama left her dwelling without peace, until, with help, she sat and stayed. Today's word.
Your line: she stayed. Today, when you want to get up from something that matters, a task, a talk, a quiet minute, stay one minute longer. Day seven hundred eighty-five.

myth: Uttama found peace the first time she sat down
four times, five times, she went out of her dwelling without peace.
Uttama went to another nun for help
a nun she could trust taught her the dhamma, and then she sat.
the poem leaves out her restlessness
the restlessness is the poem's first line.

fork.setup: you're Uttama. four, five times you've left your dwelling, restless, your thoughts out of control. what do you do next?
options: give up the robe and go home.
go to a nun you trust and listen.
lock yourself in and try harder alone.
fork.reveal: she goes to a nun she trusts, hears the teaching, and then sits in one posture until the darkness breaks.

original.note: Pali catukkhattuṃ: four times. The opening word of Uttama's verse.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nun who couldn't sit still.
what it means: restlessness counted honestly, help asked for, and then she sat and stayed.
what a scholar hears: the commentary names the nun Uttama went to as Patacara; the verse itself says only that she went to a nun she could trust.

786.title: The wick drawn down
786.hook: Patacara watches the lamp's wick pulled down and the flame go out, and is free (Therigatha, Patacara)
786.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use the image of a lamp going out when explaining nibbana, and in Theravada communities Patacara's verse is read as a picture of it, told by a woman who had known great loss.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Uttama, who left her dwelling four, five times, until she sat. Your line was she stayed. Did you stay one minute longer with something? Today, the teacher she went to. Day seven hundred eighty-six.

Night. A small hut. A clay lamp burning beside a bed. A woman sits down on the bed and takes up a needle. She reaches into the lamp, draws the wick down, and the flame goes out. In the Therigatha, that is the moment Patacara's mind comes free. The path met her before, as the woman who lost everything and became a teacher of grieving women. The commentary says she taught Uttama too. Today, Patacara's own poem, and the lamp at the center of it.
screen: `A HUT AT NIGHT.` → `A NEEDLE AND A LAMP.` → `THE FLAME GOES OUT.`

segments.voice: First, her question. The poem opens in the fields. Men plow with their plows and sow seed in the ground, and they gain wealth and support their wives and children. Then Patacara asks: I keep the precepts, I do what the Teacher taught, I'm not lazy and I'm not proud. Why haven't I come free? It's an honest complaint, and the poem keeps it. Second, the water. She washes her feet, the poem says, and watches the water run down the slope. She steadies her mind, the way a good horse is trained. The path will come back to that washing tomorrow. Third, the lamp. Then she takes a lamp and goes into her dwelling. She looks over the bed, sits down on it, takes a needle, and draws down the wick. Fourth, the word. Like the going out of the lamp, the poem says, was the release of her mind. And the Pali uses a very particular word for the lamp going out: nibbana. The same word the tradition uses for the goal of the whole path. In this poem it's not abstract at all. It's a flame in a clay lamp, and a woman with a needle, watching it go. No one blows it out. The wick is drawn down, and the flame has nothing left to hold onto. So the flame goes out. The poem doesn't explain the image. It sets the small, ordinary act of putting a lamp out for the night beside the freedom the whole path aims at, and lets them sit together.
screen: `WHY NOT ME?` · `WATER RUNNING DOWN THE SLOPE.` · `A NEEDLE DRAWS THE WICK DOWN.` · `NIBBANA: THE LAMP GOES OUT.` · then, large: `THE FLAME GOES OUT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch a flame go out. If a candle is nearby and it's safe, light it, watch it for a few breaths, and then put it out and watch the last of the smoke rise. If not, dim a lamp or a screen, or close your eyes and wait for one thought to end on its own, the way a flame ends when nothing feeds it. Don't push the thought away. Just watch it finish. Then rest in the quiet after it. The bell holds the time.
The wick drawn down. Patacara pulls a lamp's wick down with a needle, and as the flame goes out, her mind comes free. Today's word.
Your line: the flame goes out. Tonight, when you switch off the last light, pause in the dark for one breath before you move. Day seven hundred eighty-six.

myth: Patacara's poem pictures freedom as a lamp going out
like the going out of the lamp, the poem says, was the release of her mind.
the poem says she had been lazy before she came free

options: reads by it late into the night.
takes a needle and draws down the wick.

fork.reveal: she sits, takes a needle and draws down the wick. as the flame goes out, her mind comes free.

original.note: Pali nibbāna (Sanskrit nirvāṇa): the going out of a flame; the word the tradition uses for the goal of the path.

trapdoor: what you thought: a woman blowing out a candle.
what it means: a lamp's quiet going out is the picture of her freedom.
what a scholar hears: the Pali uses the same word, nibbana, for the lamp going out and for the mind's release: like the nibbana of the lamp.

sources.ref: Therigatha commentary on Uttama (Patacara as her teacher)

787.title: Wash your feet
787.hook: thirty nuns take Patacara's teaching while washing their feet (Therigatha, the thirty nuns)
787.howItsDone: Some Buddhist monasteries keep water by the door for washing the feet before entering the hall, and some Theravada teachers read the verses of Patacara and her students as a picture of practice that begins in ordinary acts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Patacara watched a lamp's wick drawn down. Your line was the flame goes out. Did you watch one go out, and stay with the dark for a moment? Today, she teaches others, and she starts with their feet. Day seven hundred eighty-seven.

Wash your feet, quickly, and sit down to one side. That's the instruction. A group of nuns has come to Patacara, the teacher whose song the path heard yesterday. The collection calls them the thirty nuns, and they have come for teaching. They might expect a long talk, or some hidden method, or a test. What she gives them starts with water and the dust of the road. Today, that instruction, and why a teacher who had been through so much would start there.
screen: `WASH YOUR FEET. SIT DOWN.` → `THE NUNS COME FOR TEACHING.` → `WATER, AND THE ROAD'S DUST.`

segments.voice: First, what she says before the feet. In the poem, Patacara points at young men pounding grain with pestles. They work hard, and with what they earn they keep a household going, wives and children. Effort is ordinary, she's saying. People pour it into a home every day. So pour it into the Buddha's teaching, which, she says, no one regrets. Second, the instruction itself. Wash your feet quickly, sit to one side, give yourself to calm of mind, and do the teaching. No ceremony. The sacred thing and the chore sit in the same sentence. Third, what the nuns do. The poem repeats her words back as deeds. They heard her. They washed their feet. They sat to one side. They gave themselves to calm. Then the night unfolds, watch by watch. In the first, the poem says, they remembered former lives. In the middle, the divine eye was made clear. In the last, they tore through the great mass of darkness. Fourth, the morning. They rise, bow at Patacara's feet, and tell her: we have done what you taught. They say they will honor her the way the thirty gods honor Indra, unbeaten in battle. Notice the shape of it. Patacara's own song tells of washing her feet before her night of release. Now she hands that same small gesture to others, and it serves them too. The water doesn't wake anyone up, and the poem never says it does. It's a doorway. You stop walking. You rinse off the road. You sit.
screen: `PESTLES, GRAIN AND A HOUSEHOLD.` · `WASH QUICKLY, SIT TO ONE SIDE.` · `THE NIGHT, WATCH BY WATCH.` · `BOWING AT HER FEET AT DAWN.` · then, large: `WASH YOUR FEET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wash your feet with attention. If you can, do it now, at a tub or a basin. If you can't, your hands will do. Feel the temperature of the water first. Then the weight of the foot, or the hand, under it. Whatever road you walked today, let it go down the drain. Patacara said quickly, and quickly here can mean without fuss, not without care. Then sit to one side, the way the nuns did, dry or damp, and let the breath settle on its own. The bell holds the time.
Wash your feet. Patacara's instruction to the nuns who came to her: rinse off the road, sit to one side, and turn the mind to calm. Today's word.
Your line: wash your feet. Today, before one thing that matters, a meal, a hard call, a quiet sit, stop and rinse your hands or feet first, and arrive. Day seven hundred eighty-seven.

788.title: The grieving mothers
788.hook: women who lost children, taught by Patacara: you don't know where he came from or went (Therigatha, the five hundred)
788.howItsDone: Theravada teachers can draw on Patacara's story and verses when they speak about grief, and Theravada memorial customs include chanting and offerings made in the name of the one who has died.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Patacara told the nuns to rinse off the road and sit. Your line was wash your feet. Did you stop and arrive before something that mattered? Today, mothers come to her carrying a grief she knows. Day seven hundred eighty-eight.

No one in the poem is named except the teacher. The collection gives these verses to a great crowd of women, and what they share is the worst thing: each of them has lost a child. They come to Patacara. The stories told about her say she lost her own children too, so whatever she says, she says from inside it. She doesn't offer the usual words. She doesn't say time heals, or that they'll feel better soon. She asks a question about a road. Today, her question, and what the mothers said after they heard it.
screen: `A CROWD OF GRIEVING MOTHERS.` → `A TEACHER WHO LOST HER OWN.` → `A QUESTION ABOUT A ROAD.`

segments.voice: First, the question. Patacara says, in substance: you don't know the road he came by, or the road he left by. You don't know where he came from, or where he went. And still you cry out, my son. Second, the turn. If you knew his road, she says, where he came from and where he went, you would not grieve like this. This is how it is for living beings. Third, the picture. He came without being asked, she says, and he left without asking leave. He came from somewhere and stayed a few days. From here he went one way, and from there another. Read slowly, it's the image of a traveler who stopped at your house. Fourth, what the mothers answer. In the poem they speak as one: she has drawn out the arrow lodged in my heart, the one so hard to see. She has taken away my grief for my son. Notice what Patacara does not say. She doesn't say the child didn't matter, or that the love was a mistake. Some readers hear the verses as hard, almost cold. Others hear a release: a mother told that her child's life ran longer than the few days she was given to see. And the arrow matters. An arrow is something lodged in you by no choice of your own, and something that can be drawn out. The poem never blames the mothers for carrying it. A woman who had carried it herself is the one who pulls it free.
screen: `WHERE DID HE COME FROM?` · `IF YOU KNEW HIS ROAD.` · `A TRAVELER WHO STAYED A FEW DAYS.` · `THE HIDDEN ARROW, DRAWN OUT.` · then, large: `WHERE HE CAME FROM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a parent who has lost a child. This one asks for gentleness, with them and with yourself. If you are that parent, simply sit with your child's name, and let the breath come and go at its own pace. Nothing more is asked. If you know such a parent, bring them to mind: their face, their kitchen, the way they say the name. You don't need to fix anything. Just hold them in attention, the way Patacara stood with the mothers who came to her. Later, if it feels right, you might send a short note that says you remembered. The bell holds the time.
The grieving mothers. Women who came to Patacara with the loss of a child, and heard her ask where he came from and where he went. Today's word.
Your line: where he came from. Today, when you think of someone you've lost, let your mind travel back before you met them, and on past where you could follow. Day seven hundred eighty-eight.

fork.setup: you're one of the mothers. Patacara has just asked where your son came from, and where he went. what do you say?

fork.reveal: in the poem the mothers answer as one: she has drawn out the hidden arrow lodged in the heart, and taken away grief for a son.

original.note: Pali salla: an arrow or dart. The mothers say Patacara drew the hidden arrow of grief from their hearts.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sad poem about loss.
what it means: Patacara asks grieving mothers about the road the child came by and left by, and they say an arrow has been drawn from their hearts.
what a scholar hears: salla, the arrow of grief, appears elsewhere in the Pali texts too, as in the Salla Sutta of the Sutta Nipata, a teaching on lamenting the dead.

sources.ref: Therigatha 6.1 (Pancasatamatta, Patacara's five hundred: her verses to the grieving mothers and their reply)

789.title: Mahapajapati's thanks
789.hook: the foster mother's song of thanks to the one she raised (Therigatha, Mahapajapati)
789.howItsDone: Buddhist communities remember Mahapajapati Gotami as the Buddha's foster mother and as the woman whose request, in the Vinaya, opened ordination to women.

segments.voice: Yesterday, grieving mothers heard Patacara ask about a child's road. Your line was where he came from. Did you let your mind travel back, before you met someone you've lost? Today, a mother of another kind, and her thanks. Day seven hundred eighty-nine.

Hero. That's the word she uses, bowing to a man she once fed as a baby. The woman is Mahapajapati Gotami. She was the sister of the Buddha's mother, Maya, and when Maya died, the texts say, she raised the boy as her own. Much later, she has gone forth herself, and her song is in the collection of the sisters. A child thanking a parent is a familiar scene. This song runs the other way. Today, a foster mother says thank you to the one she raised.
screen: `SHE CALLS HIM HERO.` → `MAYA'S SISTER RAISED HIM.` → `THANKS THAT RUN THE OTHER WAY.`

segments.voice: First, the opening. Buddha, hero, homage to you, she says, highest of beings, who freed me from suffering, and many other people too. The woman who once held him now bows. Second, the long view. In the poem she says that in lives before this one she has been a mother, a son, a father, a brother, a grandmother, wandering on without seeing how things are. Parent and child, in her telling, are parts played many times, in both directions. Who raised whom depends on where you stand. Third, a gift that goes both ways. In the Majjhima there's a teaching on offerings that begins with Mahapajapati bringing the Buddha new cloth she has made herself. He asks her to give it to the whole community. Ananda speaks up for her. She was your mother's sister, he says, your nurse, the one who fed you with her own milk when your mother died. And Ananda adds that the help ran the other way too: through the Buddha she found refuge and the teaching. The Buddha agrees, and says a debt like that is not easy to repay. Neither debt cancels the other. Fourth, the close of the song. Truly, she says, Maya gave birth to Gotama for the good of many. So she honors her sister too, the mother who didn't live to see any of it. And she says what honoring the Buddhas looks like: disciples together in harmony, energetic, steady in effort. Her thanks don't stay words. They become a picture of people still practicing.
screen: `HOMAGE TO YOU, HERO.` · `MOTHER, SON, FATHER, BROTHER.` · `A CLOTH, AND A DEBT BOTH WAYS.` · `MAYA GAVE BIRTH FOR MANY.` · then, large: `THANKS TO THE CHILD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank someone you raised, or someone who raised you. Settle, and let the breath be easy. Bring one person to mind: a parent, a grandparent, an aunt, a teacher, an older brother or sister, or a child who is grown now. Let their face come. Then find one specific thing to thank them for. Not everything. One: a meal, a ride in the rain, a hard conversation they didn't avoid. Hold it for a few breaths. If they're no longer living, thanks can still be spoken in the heart. The bell holds the time.
Mahapajapati's thanks. The foster mother's song to the one she raised: homage to you, hero, who freed me and many others. Today's word.
Your line: thanks to the child. Today, thank someone younger than you for one thing they taught you, out loud if you can. Day seven hundred eighty-nine.

790.title: Kisa Gotami's song
790.hook: her own verses: good friends, grief, and the deathless found (Therigatha, Kisa Gotami)
790.howItsDone: Some Theravada teachers tell Kisa Gotami's mustard-seed story when they speak about death and grief, and return to good friendship when they speak of walking the path with others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mahapajapati sang her thanks to the one she raised. Your line was thanks to the child. Did you thank someone younger for something they taught you? Today, a woman known for one story, singing about something else. Day seven hundred ninety.

Friends come first. That's where Kisa Gotami's own song begins, before any grief. The path met her before in the commentaries' story: the dead child carried from door to door, the mustard seed from a house where no one has died, every house with its dead. That story belongs to the commentaries. In the Therigatha, in her own verses, she puts something else ahead of it. Today, her song, in the order she sings it.
screen: `FRIENDS COME FIRST.` → `THE MUSTARD SEED: A COMMENTARY STORY.` → `HER OWN SONG, IN ORDER.`

segments.voice: First, the opening. Good friendship, she says, has been praised by the Sage. Keep company with good friends, and even a fool would grow wise. Stay close to good people; that's how wisdom grows; in their company, one is freed from every suffering. She puts this before anything else. Second, the grief. Her verses do hold loss, and terrible loss: a woman on the road, giving birth far from home, a husband found dead, children gone, a family burned on one pyre. The commentary connects these lines with Patacara; some readers hear them as Kisa Gotami's own. Either way, the song doesn't look away. It speaks of tears shed across countless lives. Third, the turn. Bereaved, she says, looked down on, I reached the deathless. I have walked the noble eightfold path. I have seen nibbana. I have looked into the mirror of the teaching. The arrow is cut out, the burden is set down. Fourth, the shape. Friends first, then grief, then freedom. Read in that order, the friends aren't decoration. And notice that even in the commentary's mustard-seed story, she isn't alone. She knocks on door after door, and every household tells her the truth: someone has died here too. The suttas have a word for this, good friendship, and in one of them, when Ananda calls it half of the holy life, the Buddha corrects him: it's the whole of it. Kisa Gotami's song seems to agree.
screen: `GOOD FRIENDS, PRAISED FIRST.` · `THE ROAD, THE PYRE, THE TEARS.` · `I HAVE SEEN THE DEATHLESS.` · `FRIENDS, THEN GRIEF, THEN FREEDOM.` · then, large: `GOOD FRIENDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a friend who stood by you. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring one friend to mind, someone who stayed when things were hard, or who told you a true thing kindly. Remember one moment with them: what they said, where you were, what the light was like. Then simply wish them well. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer. If you don't, just hold them in your attention, the way you'd keep a hand on a friend's shoulder. The bell holds the time.
Kisa Gotami's song. Her own verses in the Therigatha: good friends first, then grief, then the deathless found. Today's word.
Your line: good friends. Today, send one message to a friend who stood by you, and say plainly what it meant. Day seven hundred ninety.

what it means: in her own verses, Kisa Gotami begins with good friends, walks through grief, and ends having reached the deathless.

791.title: My hair was black
791.hook: Ambapali's song of her aging body: once lovely, now changed; the truth's word never fails (Therigatha, Ambapali)
791.carry: so it was, so it is
791.howItsDone: Reflection on the body's changes is a traditional Buddhist contemplation, and Ambapali's verses are read in Theravada settings as a picture of impermanence seen in one's own body.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kisa Gotami's own song put friends first, before grief. Your line was good friends. Did you tell a friend plainly what they meant? Today, a woman looks at her own body across the years. Day seven hundred ninety-one.

Black as bees, curled at the tips. That's how Ambapali remembers her hair. The path met her before as the courtesan of Vesali who hosted the Buddha for a meal and gave his community her mango grove. In the Therigatha she is an old nun, and her song walks down her own body, from her hair to her feet, then and now. Every verse ends the same way, and that refrain is today's lesson.
screen: `BLACK AS BEES.` → `A COURTESAN, THEN A NUN.` → `ONE REFRAIN, EVERY VERSE.`

segments.voice: First, then and now. My hair was black, she says, the color of bees, curled at the tips. Now, with age, it's like coarse bark fiber. And then the refrain: not otherwise is the word of the one who speaks the truth. So it was. So it is. Second, the walk. She goes on, part by part. Eyes that shone like jewels, now dim. A voice sweet as a cuckoo's in the forest, now faltering. Teeth once bright, now broken. Each verse holds a then and a now, and each closes with the same line. The repeating is part of the teaching; it settles in, verse by verse. Third, who is speaking. This is the woman who, in the sutta of the Buddha's last journey, wouldn't give up a meal with him for all of Vesali, and then gave his community her grove. A woman who knew what beauty and wealth could buy is the one telling us, steadily, what time did. Fourth, the tone. Some readers hear grief in the song. Others hear something calmer: no complaint, no shame, only accuracy. Near the end she says this body is like an old house with its plaster falling away. And the refrain says the Buddha's word holds: things change. In her mouth that isn't a curse. It's a teaching confirmed, by her own skin.
screen: `BLACK HAIR, NOW LIKE BARK.` · `EYES, VOICE, TEETH: THEN AND NOW.` · `ONCE THE COURTESAN OF VESALI.` · `AN OLD HOUSE, PLASTER FALLING.` · then, large: `SO IT WAS, SO IT IS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at an old photograph. Find one of yourself, on your phone or in a drawer, or call one up from memory. Look at it the way Ambapali looked at herself. Hair then, hair now. Face then, face now. Don't argue with it. Don't praise it. Just name it softly: so it was. Then feel the body you're in right now, breathing, sitting, here. So it is. Let the two sit side by side. The bell holds the time.
My hair was black. Ambapali's song of her own body, then and now, with every verse closing on the truth-speaker's word. Today's word.

Your line: so it was, so it is. This week the sisters sang of a nun who finally stayed, a flame gone out, washed feet, grieving mothers, a foster mother's thanks, and good friends. Today, catch your reflection once and say the line, with no verdict. Day seven hundred ninety-one.

original.note: Pali sacca: truth. Ambapali's refrain calls the Buddha the one who speaks the truth.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sad poem about getting old.
what it means: Ambapali walks through her own body, then and now, and every verse confirms the truth-speaker's word: so it was.
what a scholar hears: the refrain names the Buddha as the speaker of truth; her own body becomes the evidence for his teaching that conditioned things change.
